text:
I am from Pakistan, and my grandfather was originally from Amritsar, India. During the migration of 1947, he came to Punjab, Pakistan. He was only 24 years old at the time, with a wife and two young children. During the violence and chaos of Partition, his wife was killed and his children went missing. He lived to be around 100 years old, but he never forgot that pain.

So many times, he shared his memories with us—his grandchildren, my siblings, and cousins. While watching “Main Wapis Aaoonga,” I could not control my tears. This movie touched me so deeply that, for a moment, it felt as if someone had taken me back into my grandfather’s past. Everything he used to tell us came alive in front of my eyes—the pain, the separation, the helplessness, and the memories he carried with him for the rest of his life.

I cried not only because of the movie, but because somewhere within it, I could see my grandfather’s story too. It brought back his words, his emotions, and the grief he carried silently for decades.

I must say, this movie is truly a masterpiece and a deeply moving tribute to all those who lost their loved ones during Partition—people who were separated from their families, their homes, and a part of themselves forever. Some wounds may belong to the past, but they continue to live in the hearts and memories of generations.

This film touched me from the heart and soul. ❤

text:
I have always been deeply moved by the fact that once, we were one country. Today, India and Pakistan often see each other as enemies—India wants to defeat Pakistan, Pakistan wants to defeat India. But there was a time when we lived together, shared the same culture, the same history, the same streets, and the same memories.

I came home from work today and watched this movie. I’m only 21, and honestly, I couldn’t sleep after watching it. My ancestors remained in India, so I never personally experienced the pain of Partition. Yet the suffering shown in this movie affected me deeply. I can’t even imagine what the people who actually went through it must have felt.

I sincerely urge my fellow Indians: please don't let hatred and misconceptions about another community or another country consume us. Partition happened, borders were drawn, and today we have separate nations. Let us accept that reality and choose to live peacefully.

Because every time we create a religious conflict, spread hatred, or justify violence in the name of identity, we are indirectly saying that the people responsible for Partition were right.

They weren't.

The greatest way to prove that Partition did not have to define our future is to choose peace today.

We cannot change history. But we can decide what kind of history we create from here.

And yet, my parents survived.

They picked up the broken pieces, endured their pain, and somehow built a beautiful life for us. They carried wounds they rarely spoke about, while giving us a childhood filled with love, safety, and hope.

Today, I understand them a little more.

Respect to my parents. ❤️
They suffered so much, yet they chose to build a life.

Some stories are not just history.
They live quietly inside families, passed from one generation to another.

text:
When Words Fall Short

I honestly don’t know how to put this into words.

Main Vaapas Ayunga is one of those rare experiences where, after the credits roll, you are left sitting quietly—trying to process what you just witnessed. I am overwhelmed by the screenplay, the performances, the music, the emotions, and the sheer magic of the entire film.

There is something deeply haunting and beautiful about it. It doesn’t merely tell a story; it makes you feel one. And that song… it left me speechless. Some songs you listen to, and some songs stay somewhere inside you long after they end.

Imtiaz Ali has created something truly magical here. And with A. R. Rahman’s music breathing life into that magic, the film becomes something far beyond cinema.

I have watched it twice in a single day, and somehow, I still feel I haven’t completely absorbed it.

There are films you watch.
There are films you remember.
And then there are films that quietly become a part of you.

Main Vaapas Ayunga is the third kind.

What a masterpiece. What a feeling. What magic.
Hats off, Imtiaz Ali and A. R. Rahman. ❤️
